title: Fibre care: linen yarn
subtitle: Washing, softening, and storing crochet worked in linen or linen-blend yarn
excerpt: Linen yarn is stiff when new and becomes softer and more pliable with repeated washing. It is one of the most durable yarn fibres for crochet and is well-suited to machine washing, though it benefits from a gentle cycle and cool temperatures to avoid shrinking in the first wash.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework, 1886, Project Gutenberg #20776. Contemporary fibre care references.

glossaryTerms.definition: Yarn spun from the fibres of the flax plant. Stiff and slightly rough when new, but softens considerably with use and washing. Strong, durable, and resistant to bacteria.
Plant fibre taken from the stem of a plant rather than from seeds or fruit. Linen (from flax), hemp, and ramie are the most common bast fibres used in yarn.

content.text: spun from flax. New linen is stiff and can feel scratchy; it becomes progressively softer and more drapey with each wash. This means a finished linen crochet piece will look and feel different after its first few uses than it did fresh off the hook. This improvement is expected and normal.
Linen tolerates machine washing, which distinguishes it from wool and silk. However, the first wash is the highest-risk one because linen can shrink by up to 5 to 10% if the water is too hot.
First wash: hand-wash in cool water, 30°C, with a gentle detergent. This controls the conditions for the potentially significant first-wash shrink.
Subsequent washes: machine wash on a gentle or delicates cycle at 30 to 40°C. Linen can tolerate 40°C without significant further shrinking once it has had its first wash.
Use a standard mild detergent. Linen is a plant fibre and is not damaged by the alkalis that harm wool and silk.
Dry flat for garments and shaped pieces to prevent them from stretching on a hanger while wet.
Flat items like table runners and dishcloths can be line-dried or tumble-dried on a low heat setting.
To soften a stiff linen piece quickly, place it in the tumble dryer on low heat with a damp cloth for 10 minutes. The steam effect softens the fibres faster than air drying alone.
Linen can be ironed while still slightly damp on a medium setting. Ironing when damp relaxes the fibres and produces a noticeably softer result than ironing dry.

Linen responds well to wet blocking. Soak the piece, pin it to the correct dimensions on a blocking mat, and leave to dry. Linen holds a blocked shape well once dry, producing crisp, open stitches in lace patterns. The fibre does not bloom like wool when blocked, but the structure of the stitch becomes more defined.

items.symptom: The piece shrank more than expected after the first wash
items.cause: The wash temperature was too high, or the piece was tumble-dried on a high heat setting.
items.fix: Soak the piece in warm water again and ease it gently back to its original dimensions by pulling from all sides while wet. Pin to a blocking mat and dry flat. Linen can be eased back toward its pre-wash size while wet but not after it has dried.

items.symptom: The finished piece is very stiff and uncomfortable to use
items.cause: Linen is naturally stiff when new and has not yet had enough washes to soften.
items.fix: Wash the piece two to three times and it will soften noticeably. Using the tumble dryer on low heat with a damp cloth speeds up the process.

items.symptom: The linen yarn is fraying at the cut end
items.cause: Linen is a spun fibre and the cut end of the yarn will unravel unless it is secured.
items.fix: Weave in linen ends over a longer distance than you would for wool (at least 5 cm), going in two directions. Linen does not felt into the fabric the way wool does, so the end must be mechanically anchored.

content.text: Wash a gauge swatch in the project yarn before starting any linen piece. Measure the swatch before and after its first wash to understand exactly how much the yarn shrinks in the first wash. This tells you whether to make adjustments to the pattern dimensions before you start the full piece.
